overview.title: 📖 Overview: Reconciling Sources, Then a New Chapter
overview.subtitle: Bekhorot 26a–26b
overview.hebrewSource: עַד כַּמָּה יִשְׂרָאֵל חַיָּיבִין לִיטַּפֵּל בִּבְכוֹר?
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: The daf completes the sugya on shed and plucked firstborn wool by having Rava reconcile three different tannaitic readings of exactly when Akavya ben Mahalalel and the Rabbis disagree — over a slaughtered animal, a naturally deceased one, or both. A parallel dispute over what counts as wool 'not part of the fleece' follows, before the chapter closes. A new mishna then opens fresh territory: how many days must an Israelite personally tend a firstborn animal before handing it to a priest, with the Gemara tracing that requirement back to a dense verse also used to derive the redemption age of a firstborn son. The daf ends with a related concern — priests, Levites, and the poor may not be paid for ordinary labor with teruma or tithes, a practice serious enough to invoke a biblical death penalty, even though the Sages stopped short of imposing an additional penalty of their own.

slides.title: 🧶 Three Ways to Read the Wool Dispute
slides.subtitle: Rava unifies the tanna kama, Rabbi Yehuda, and Rabbi Yosei versions of the same baraita

boxes.title: Tanna Kama
items: Akavya and the Rabbis disagree in BOTH cases — a slaughtered animal and one that died naturally
The baraita mentions 'died' specifically to show how far Akavya's leniency extends

boxes.title: Rabbi Yehuda
items: If the animal died, everyone agrees the wool is forbidden
They disagree only in the case of a slaughtered animal

boxes.title: Rabbi Yosei — the accepted halakha
items: If the animal was slaughtered, everyone agrees the wool is permitted
They disagree only in the case of a naturally deceased animal
Rav Naḥman rules the halakha follows this version, based on the parallel mishna in tractate Eduyyot

callout.label: Common thread:
callout.text: All three agree slaughter and natural death are treated differently — they only disagree about which case is actually disputed.

slides.title: 🐑 Wool Dangling From a Firstborn: Two Definitions
slides.subtitle: What exactly counts as wool that 'does not appear to be part of the fleece'?
rows: Any strand whose root is turned outward, facing away from the body
Any strand not compressed together with the rest of the fleece — one that sticks out when the fleece is pressed down
No fleece is ever entirely free of loose, dangling hairs — Rav Natan's stricter standard would make the lenient ruling meaningless in practice

callout.label: Practical effect:
callout.text: Reish Lakish's more workable definition ensures the mishna's leniency for dangling-but-attached wool actually applies in real cases.

slides.title: 🕐 How Long Must an Owner Raise a Firstborn?
slides.subtitle: New mishna, new chapter

nodes.content: ❓ How long must an Israelite personally tend a firstborn before giving it to the priest?

columns.label: Small animal
columns.content: 30 days (Rabbi Yosei: 3 months, due to the extra effort of raising it)

nodes.content: 🚫 If the priest demands it early, the owner may not give it to him — this looks like paying the priest for his labor with a sacred gift

columns.label: Blemished firstborn
columns.content: If the priest wants it early to EAT it — permitted

columns.label: Unblemished, Temple standing
columns.content: If the priest wants it early to SACRIFICE it — permitted

callout.label: Underlying concern:
callout.text: Handing over the animal early, without a legitimate reason, would look like an improper trade of labor for sacred goods.

slides.title: 📜 Deriving Thirty and Fifty Days From One Verse
slides.subtitle: Exodus 22:28–29 links firstborn sons and firstborn animals

steps.content: 1️⃣ The verse juxtaposes 'you shall give Me your firstborn sons' (redeemed at 30 days) with 'so shall you do with your oxen and your sheep'
2️⃣ Rav Kahana's first attempt: match each animal to its nearby phrase in the verse — but the Gemara challenges why the correspondence should run one way and not the other
3️⃣ That attempt is set aside as inconclusive

4️⃣ Rava's alternative: the extra word 'תַּעֲשֶׂה' (you shall do) teaches an ADDITIONAL act of care specifically for oxen — both sheep and oxen start from the son's 30-day baseline, but oxen require more
5️⃣ Why not double to 60 days, then? The Torah handed the precise figure to the Sages to determine — they set it at 50

callout.label: Structure:
callout.text: A single verse anchors both time periods, but only the Sages' own judgment fixes the exact additional number of days.

slides.title: 💰 Paying Temple Workers With Sacred Produce
slides.subtitle: Why the priest can't simply take the firstborn early
rows: A priest who takes the firstborn early looks like one who 'helps at the threshing floor' just to be given teruma — an improper labor-for-sacred-goods trade
Priests, Levites, and the poor who help at a shepherd's home, threshing floor, or slaughterhouse may not be paid with teruma or tithe as wages
The produce is considered profaned; Numbers 18:32 even threatens death for desecrating sacred items in this way
The Sages feared people would then mistakenly separate tithes again from produce already validly tithed, over-tithing exempt produce

callout.label: Bigger picture:
callout.text: The same concern — sacred status used as informal payment for labor — underlies both the firstborn-timing rule and the teruma/tithe wages prohibition.

summary.principle: Precise timing and precise definitions — of when a dispute applies, what counts as attached wool, and how long an owner must care for a firstborn — protect the line between legitimate caretaking and using sacred status as informal payment.

columns.content: 📜 The verse anchoring these periods ties firstborn animals to the redemption of a firstborn son
💰 Temple workers may never be paid in teruma or tithes for ordinary labor

quiz.q: According to the version of the baraita that Rav Naḥman rules is halakha (Rabbi Yosei's version), in which case do Akavya ben Mahalalel and the Rabbis actually disagree?
o: Only when the animal was slaughtered
Only when the animal died naturally, not slaughtered
In both cases equally
They never actually disagree
quiz.e: According to Rabbi Yosei's version, which Rav Naḥman rules as halakha, everyone agrees the wool is permitted if the animal was slaughtered; Akavya and the Rabbis disagree only in the case of an animal that died by other means.

quiz.q: According to Rabbi Ile'a, why does Reish Lakish reject Rav Natan bar Oshaya's stricter definition of wool 'not part of the fleece'?
o: Because Rav Natan's definition contradicts a verse
Because no fleece is ever entirely free of loose, dangling hairs, so that stricter standard would make the mishna's leniency meaningless
Because Reish Lakish disagreed with Rav Natan on unrelated matters
Because the stricter definition only applies to blemished animals
quiz.e: Rabbi Ile'a explains that if wool sticking out when pressed were always forbidden, since some dangling hairs are unavoidable in any fleece, the mishna's leniency would never actually apply — so Reish Lakish adopts a more workable definition.

quiz.q: According to the new mishna, how long must an owner tend a small-animal firstborn before giving it to the priest, and what is one exception allowing earlier transfer?
o: 15 days; no exceptions exist
30 days; the priest may take it earlier if the firstborn is blemished and he wants to eat it
60 days; the priest may never take it earlier
30 days; an exception only applies to large animals
quiz.e: The mishna sets 30 days for a small animal (Rabbi Yosei says 3 months). One clear exception: if the firstborn is blemished and the priest wants to eat it, the owner may give it to him earlier.

quiz.q: According to Rava, what does the extra word 'תַּעֲשֶׂה' (you shall do) in Exodus 22:29 teach about a firstborn ox?
o: That oxen are entirely exempt from the firstborn mitzva
That an additional period of care, beyond the 30-day baseline shared with a firstborn son, is required specifically for oxen
That oxen must be tended for exactly 30 days like sheep
That oxen may be given to the priest immediately
quiz.e: Rava explains that the extra word 'you shall do' adds an additional act of caretaking specifically required for oxen, beyond the 30-day baseline derived from the redemption of a firstborn son — with the exact additional amount (bringing the total to 50 days) left to the Sages to determine.

quiz.q: According to Rav Sheshet, why may a priest not take a firstborn animal from its owner before the required tending period has ended, even if the owner is willing?
o: Because the animal would not yet be old enough to be kosher
Because it would look like the priest is being paid for labor (like helping at a threshing floor) with a sacred gift
Because the Torah explicitly forbids any early transfer under all circumstances
Because the priest is not yet permitted to own animals
quiz.e: Rav Sheshet explains that a priest collecting the firstborn early would appear similar to a priest who 'assists at the threshing floor' specifically to receive teruma — an improper arrangement where sacred goods function as payment for labor.
